title: Version control and Git
idea: Version control records every change to a project as a history you can read, compare and undo. Git is a free, open-source version-control system.
points: A repository is a project folder plus its complete history.
A commit is a saved snapshot of your files, with a message.
A branch is a separate line of work that you can merge back later.
Git is distributed: a normal clone copies the whole repository, history included.

steps.caption: Ada saves two commits, A and B. They live in her own copy of the repository.
She pushes them, which uploads her commits to a shared server. It now holds the same history.
Bob clones the repository: a full copy of it, every commit included.
The server goes down. Both laptops still hold the complete history.
Ada keeps working. Commit C is saved on her own machine, with no server needed.

pitfalls: Git is not GitHub. Git is the tool; GitHub is one website that hosts repositories.
Renamed copies of a folder record nothing about what changed or why.

options: Git needs a server to save a commit
Only the server keeps the history
A normal clone holds the full history
Your files are split between developers
quiz.why: Each clone is a complete repository with every commit, so you can commit, read history and branch without a network.

takeaway: Git saves snapshots as commits, and every clone holds the whole history.

starters: Do I need GitHub to use Git?
What problem does version control solve for a team?
Is Git the only version control system?
